title: MLflow, experiments and reproducibility
summary: Read a run as evidence, compare runs that changed one thing, rerun from the record or refuse, package a model with its signature and environment, and promote a registered version by evidence.
objectives: Read and log a run's parameters, metrics, datasets, artifacts and model, and say what each can and cannot prove.
Decide whether two runs are comparable and whether a run can be reproduced from its record, and expose one that cannot.
Package a model with a signature and environment, apply a versioned contract, and promote a version by moving an alias on evidence.
Separate the duties of open-source MLflow from those of Databricks-managed MLflow with models in Unity Catalog.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
A run is the record behind a number
Datasets pin rows, not their quality
Versions, aliases and promotion by evidence
Mistakes that make a record misleading

questions.prompt: The lab's time-split-C-1 and time-split-C-0.01 runs share training digest 4950f73b and differ only in C. The time-split-leaky run shares the digest and differs from C-1 only in features. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both pairs are comparable; the second isolates the post-event column.
options.rationale: Both pairs trained on the same rows and changed one parameter, so each difference belongs to that parameter: the leak alone moves accuracy from 0.8056 to 1.0.

options.text: Only the first pair, because a different feature list means different data rows.
options.rationale: The logged dataset holds every column of the same rows, so the digest is shared; the features parameter says which columns the model read.

options.text: Neither pair, because runs whose metrics differ cannot be compared.
options.rationale: Differing metrics are what a comparison measures; comparability is about the rows and the parameters, not the outcome.

options.text: Both pairs, which makes the leaky run the stronger candidate for promotion.
options.rationale: Comparable is not valid: the leaky run reads a column written after the fault and fails the evidence gate before its metrics are read.

questions.prompt: A model logged with a six-column double signature is loaded with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model in MLflow 3.16.1 and receives the six columns plus repair_minutes. What happens?

options.text: It raises a schema enforcement error that names repair_minutes.
options.rationale: Errors come from missing required inputs and unsafe type conversions; an extra column does not raise, which is why the contract checks unexpected inputs itself.

options.text: It uses repair_minutes, because pyfunc matches columns by their position.
options.rationale: Columns are matched by name; a reordered frame is accepted for that reason, and an unnamed extra column is ignored.

options.text: It refuses to load the model until the signature is updated to seven columns.
options.rationale: Loading is unaffected; enforcement happens on each predict call, not at load time.

options.text: It predicts, ignoring the extra column with a logged warning.
options.rationale: Observed in the lab: enforcement checks for missing and unsafe inputs, and an input the signature does not name is dropped with a warning.

questions.prompt: Version 1 of cinderline-oven-fault carries the alias candidate. A reproduced rerun is registered, the alias is moved to it, and then moved back. What changed?

options.text: Version 1 was overwritten with the files of version 2.
options.rationale: A registered version's files do not change; a new registration creates a new number instead.

options.text: Version 1's stage moved from Staging to Production and back.
options.rationale: No stage was involved; aliases and tags replace stages, and Unity Catalog does not support stages at all.

options.text: Only which version the alias names; both versions remain.
options.rationale: Versions are fixed registrations; the alias is a mutable pointer, so a rollback is moving it back.

options.text: Version 2 was deleted when the alias moved back to version 1.
options.rationale: Moving an alias never deletes a version; version 2 stays in the registry without an alias.

cards.prompt: What does one MLflow run record, and which store keeps each part?
cards.answer: Parameters, metrics, tags and dataset references go to the backend store; files such as reports and the model directory go to the artifact store.
cards.explanation: In the lab's file store the split is visible as folders: params/, metrics/, tags/ and inputs/ beside artifacts/ and the logged model's own directory. Losing the artifact store keeps the numbers but loses the model and the check reports behind them.

cards.prompt: What happens when code logs a new value for a parameter the run already recorded?
cards.answer: MLflow 3.16.1 raises an error saying parameter values cannot be changed; logging the same value again is accepted.
cards.explanation: Parameters describe choices made before the run, so the record keeps the first value. That protects the record from being edited into agreement with a result; a different choice belongs in a new run, which is also what makes a comparison possible.

cards.prompt: Why log the whole training rows as the dataset rather than only the model's columns?
cards.answer: Then the digest identifies the rows, so runs with different feature lists still share it and can be compared.
cards.explanation: In the lab, the C = 1, C = 0.01 and leaky runs share digest 4950f73b because they read the same 672 rows; the features parameter records which columns each model used. Logging only chosen columns would make a feature ablation look like a change of data.

cards.prompt: Does a matching dataset digest show that the training data was correct?
cards.answer: No; a digest fingerprints content, and in MLflow 3.16.1 at most the first 10,000 rows, and says nothing about validity.
cards.explanation: The leaky run had a complete record with a digest and still trained on repair_minutes, written after the fault. Validity comes from checks such as the availability dictionary and the split report, whose outputs the run should keep as artifacts. A logged run does not certify data quality.

cards.prompt: When may you attribute the metric difference between two runs to one cause?
cards.answer: When they trained on the same rows, shown by the same training digest, and differ in exactly one deliberate parameter.
cards.explanation: C = 1 against C = 0.01 isolates regularization and C = 1 against the leaky run isolates the post-event column. The random split changes the rows and three parameters at once, and the hero logged no dataset, so neither supports a single-cause reading.

cards.prompt: Why does never-warn beat every honest model on accuracy in the oven experiment?
cards.answer: Faults are 18 of 288 test rows, so predicting no fault is right 270 times: accuracy 0.9375 with recall 0.
cards.explanation: Accuracy rewards the majority class. The contract therefore reads recall, precision and warnings a day, which map to missed faults and to an inspection round that holds two ovens. Logging baselines as runs keeps that comparison in the same table.

cards.prompt: What must a run record so that it can be rerun from its record alone?
cards.answer: Every parameter the code reads, including the seed and split cut-off, the feature list, the training dataset and the library versions.
cards.explanation: The lab's reproduction step reads C, class weight, iterations, seed, split, cut-off day, features and the scikit-learn version, finds the training digest, and refuses naming each gap when one is missing. With all of them, the clean rerun matched every metric bit for bit.

cards.prompt: Two executions of the hero's code left identical records. What does that prove?
cards.answer: Its result depended on something the record does not hold, the unseeded split, so the record cannot reproduce it.
cards.explanation: Both records hold only model=logistic_regression, yet one test set held 20 faults and the other 18. When identical records carry different numbers, the numbers belong to hidden state. The right response is to refuse the run, not to guess a seed.

cards.prompt: What does the list of flavors in an MLmodel file let a consumer do?
cards.answer: Load the same model either through the generic python_function interface or with the library's own flavor, such as sklearn.
cards.explanation: python_function is the interface MLflow tools use for any Python model, and it is where signature enforcement happens. The sklearn flavor returns the fitted pipeline itself. In the lab the MLmodel file also recorded skops serialization, the scikit-learn version and the model ID.

cards.prompt: Which input change does pyfunc schema enforcement let through, and what catches it?
cards.answer: An extra column the signature does not name; a contract check for unexpected inputs catches it.
cards.explanation: In MLflow 3.16.1 a renamed column and an int64 column were refused, a reordered frame was accepted, and an extra repair_minutes column was ignored with a warning. A contract that lists its inputs rejects the extra column by name before anyone sends a post-event field.

cards.prompt: Why can a recorded library version stop a rerun before it starts?
cards.answer: Because a rerun on a different scikit-learn version is a different computation, and the lab refuses to call it a reproduction.
cards.explanation: The model's requirements.txt and python_env.yaml pin the environment that loads it, and the run records scikit-learn as a parameter. A copy of the clean record claiming 1.8.0 was refused on a 1.9.1 installation, before any training happened.

cards.prompt: In a registry, what moves when a model is promoted and what stays fixed?
cards.answer: The alias moves to a version; each version's files and source run stay fixed, so a rollback is moving the alias back.
cards.explanation: Registering the reproduced rerun created version 2 with identical predictions, the alias moved to it and then back to version 1, and neither version changed. Consumers that load models:/cinderline-oven-fault@candidate follow the alias; nothing is deployed by moving it.

cards.prompt: What does the evidence gate check before any metric of a candidate run is read?
cards.answer: A time split, a recorded seed, a logged training dataset, a feature list without post-event columns and a signature matching the contract.
cards.explanation: Three runs with attractive numbers stopped there: the random split, the leaky run and the hero, whose 1.0 accuracy was never read. Only runs that pass the gate meet the thresholds, and the decision file records every reason.

cards.prompt: Which duties does Databricks take over from an open-source MLflow setup, and which stay?
cards.answer: Hosting, access control and a Unity Catalog registry move to the platform; choosing the run, the contract and data checks stay.
cards.explanation: Open-source MLflow leaves the tracking server, its stores and their security to you. On Databricks, experiments carry permission levels and models live in Unity Catalog with three-level names, privileges and aliases. No platform decides which run deserves an alias or certifies a logged dataset.
